label: Hohensalzburg
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).

text.description:
Hohensalzburg Fortress is the big white-walled fortress that sits on the Festungsberg above Salzburg, at an altitude of 506 m. It is about 250 m long and 150 m wide, which makes it one of the largest medieval castles in Europe. Building began in 1077, and the prince-archbishops kept adding to it over the following centuries. The ring walls and towers date from 1462, and the outer bastions were finished in the 17th century. It was never taken by force. It also has the Reisszug, an early funicular railway first described in 1515 and probably the oldest working railway in the world. The Festungsbahn funicular has run up from the town since 1892.

It photographs well because the hill gives it a ready-made pedestal. The walls and towers sit in one long line along the ridge, so the whole outline reads clearly even from some distance. The phone icon on the map is about 540 m south of the subject. That is far enough to fit the fortress and the hillside below it in one frame, but too far for detail without zooming. Take one wide shot to show the setting, then move in with the zoom to pick out the towers and the line of the walls. Keep the horizon level, and watch for trees or lamp posts cutting across the lower edge of the picture.
text.geographic_location: The fortress stands on the Festungsberg hill, overlooking the city of Salzburg, Austria.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 540 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the fortress and the hill together. Then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the walls and towers. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, because it makes the fortress look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 540 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. This distance suits the default lens (1x) for the whole scene and the zoom for close-ups.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the line of the walls on the upper third line, with the hillside filling the rest. Keep the horizon level. Take one shot with the whole hill and one zoomed shot of the towers and walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fortress walls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the white walls keep their detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands when you zoom, and take two or three frames to be sure of one sharp one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late morning to afternoon is likely to suit best, because the sun should be behind you and shining on the fortress's south-facing walls. On an overcast day the walls will look flatter, so zoom in on the towers for more interest.

text.access_note: The stand-here point is a viewing place for the fortress; the fortress itself may be ticketed or have restricted areas, so check the official site before you go.

label: Mirabell Gardens
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).

text.description:
Mirabell Palace and its formal gardens sit just north of Salzburg's old town and are one of the most popular tourist attractions in Salzburg. The gardens are laid out in neat geometric patterns, with clipped boxwood, mythological statues and a hedge theatre, so there are strong lines and colour to build a photo around. The palace itself is pale and Neoclassical, and it closes the view at the far end of the garden.

The palace dates from about 1606, when Prince-Archbishop Wolf Dietrich built it as a pleasure palace. It was rebuilt in Baroque style in the 1720s and given its present Neoclassical look around 1818, after a fire. The gardens were planned from 1687, and the statue groups by Ottavio Mosto date from 1690. Today the palace houses the mayor's office and city departments, and the Marble Hall is used for concerts and weddings. Film fans may also recognise the Pegasus fountain and the steps from the 'Do-Re-Mi' scene in The Sound of Music.

For photos, use the lines of the paths and flowerbeds to lead the eye towards the palace. Keep the phone level using the gridlines, and look for a gap between visitors before you take the shot.
text.geographic_location: Mirabell Palace stands in the city of Salzburg, just north of the medieval city walls and close to the Salzach river. It is part of the Historic Centre of the City of Salzburg World Heritage Site.
text.directions_text: Start from Salzburg's old town and head north, out beyond the line of the medieval city walls, towards the Salzach river. The palace and gardens lie on that side of the old town. The phone icon on the map is about 180 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the palace with the garden in front of it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole garden layout in the frame. Use telephoto (2x or more) for statues, fountain details and the palace front without people in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 180 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the palace on the upper line, with a path or a flowerbed edge running into the frame from the bottom. Keep the phone level so the palace front stays straight. For a second picture, move in close with 2x zoom and frame a statue or a clipped hedge against the palace.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the pale walls keep their detail. Panorama mode can work for the wide garden if you hold the phone steady and wait for passers-by to clear the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually the quietest time, and the light is softer. Later in the day the gardens tend to be busier, so be ready to wait for gaps in the crowd.

text.access_note: The gardens are a public attraction, but check the official site before you go for current access rules, and for any visits inside the palace.

text.description:
Mozart's Birthplace is the tall house at No. 9 Getreidegasse where Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born on 27 January 1756. His family rented the third-floor flat from 1747 to 1773. The building has been a museum since 1880, with his childhood violin and the clavichord he used to compose The Magic Flute. It is also known as the Hagenauerhaus, after the family who owned it from 1703.

It photographs well because it sits in a narrow shopping street, so the tall façade, the shopfronts and the busy lane all fit into one frame. A small detail is worth a second shot: on the doorway, a coiled serpent in a lion's mouth records the court apothecary who bought the house in 1585. The house itself dates from the 12th century.

Start with a wider shot that shows the street leading towards the house, then walk up for a closer picture of the façade and the doorway. Because the lane is tight, you will usually have to shoot upwards or at an angle, so keep your phone level and use the gridlines to stop the walls leaning. Passers-by are part of the scene here, so wait a moment for a gap if you want a cleaner frame.
text.geographic_location: On Getreidegasse (No. 9) in the centre of Salzburg, among the shops and narrow buildings of the old town.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops listed for this spot, so head for Getreidegasse in the centre of Salzburg. Look for No. 9 on Getreidegasse. The phone icon on the map is about 140 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot, and switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane is too narrow to fit the whole façade. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the doorway and its serpent-and-lion symbol.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 140 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a wider picture there that shows the approach, then walk east for about 2 minutes to No. 9 Getreidegasse for close-ups of the façade and doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone upright, so the vertical walls stay straight. Frame the house with the lane running into the picture, and include a little of the neighbouring buildings to show the scale. For a detail shot, use zoom on the doorway rather than walking right up to it, so you do not block the entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the façade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky looks washed out. Wait for a gap in the crowd before pressing the shutter, or use a Live Photo and pick the cleanest frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late evening usually means fewer people in the lane, which makes it easier to get a clear shot of the façade.

text.access_note: The building is a museum, so entry is likely to be ticketed; check the official site before you go. The façade can be photographed from the public street.

text.description: Schloss Leopoldskron is a rococo palace on the edge of a lake, the Leopoldskroner Weiher, in the quiet southern part of Salzburg. It photographs well because the pale building sits right at the water's edge, so you can include the lake, the lawns and the trees in one frame. Prince-Archbishop Leopold Anton von Firmian had it built in 1736 beside an existing pond. In 1918 the theatre director Max Reinhardt, co-founder of the Salzburg Festival, bought it and spent about twenty years restoring it. Since 1947 it has been home to the Salzburg Global Seminar, and since 2014 the palace and the neighbouring Meierhof have also run as a hotel. Film fans should know that the palace itself never appears in The Sound of Music. Some scenes were shot on the neighbouring Meierhof grounds, using replicas of the palace's terrace and gate. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m west of the subject. That is far enough to fit the whole 74 m-wide building into a photo without any special effort. Take a wide shot first, then move in closer for the façade. Because the palace is privately run, respect the hotel's private grounds and any signs, and check the official site before you go if you hope to see more of the grounds.
text.geographic_location: Schloss Leopoldskron lies in Leopoldskron-Moos, a southern district of the city of Salzburg, on the shore of the lake Leopoldskroner Weiher. The neighbouring Meierhof building stands right beside it.
text.directions_text: Check a local journey planner for the best way to reach the Leopoldskron-Moos area in the south of Salzburg. From there the palace is 233 m to the east, a short walk away. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the palace together with the lake and trees around it. Then try 2x or 3x on your phone to tighten the frame on the façade and cut out clutter. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sky and water, as it will make the palace look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 230 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Keep your phone level so the building does not lean, and respect the hotel's private grounds and any signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the palace along one of the vertical lines, with the water filling the lower third. Include some trees or grass at the edge of the frame to give a sense of depth. Take one wide shot of the whole setting and one closer shot of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the pale walls keep their detail. Turn on Live Photos if there are ripples on the water, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: In the afternoon the sun is in the west, behind you as you look east, so it should light the side of the palace facing you. Early morning on a calm day may give a reflection in the lake.

text.access_note: The palace is a privately run hotel and seminar centre, so check the official site before you go to find out what is open to visitors.

label: Salzburg Cathedral

text.description: Salzburg Cathedral is the big Baroque church at the heart of the Old Town, dedicated to Saint Rupert and Saint Vergilius. The façade is bright Untersberg marble, framed by two towers and topped with a curved gable. The body of the church is dark grey stone, so the pale front stands out well against it. It photographs well because the cathedral, the Residenz and St Peter's Abbey form one enclosed square, entered through three open arches. That gives you a natural frame for your shots. The present building was consecrated in 1628 and replaced an older church that was badly damaged in 1598. It is 142 metres long and 33 metres high at the crossing. Mozart was baptised here in 1756. In the middle of Domplatz stands the Maria Immaculata column, put up between 1766 and 1771. From the centre of the arcades at the back of the square it lines up with the middle of the façade, and the golden crown above the central window appears to sit over the figure. The building is far too large to fit in a single frame from close in, so decide whether you want the whole front, the square, or a detail such as the statues of the saints between the portals or the evangelists along the balustrade.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral is in the Altstadt (Old Town) of Salzburg, beside Residenzplatz and Domplatz. It stands next to the Residenz and St Peter's Abbey.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Altstadt, the Old Town, and look for Domplatz and Residenzplatz, where the cathedral stands. If you are coming from elsewhere in Salzburg, head to the Old Town and walk the last stretch. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the façade, the towers and some of the square, because the cathedral is very large. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the front. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the statues, the gable and the golden crown.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. You are close, so the ultra-wide is the lens to reach for first. For the column-and-façade alignment, walk back to the centre of the arcades at the back of Domplatz.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central portal and the middle window up with the vertical centre line, so the symmetrical façade looks straight. Include the Maria Immaculata column in the foreground if you can, with the crown above the central window behind it. Hold the phone level and keep the towers upright, since tilting upwards makes them lean inwards. For a second shot, zoom in on the saints' statues between the three portals.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the marble façade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the pale stone keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out. If the arches frame you in shade, try a Live Photo to catch a moment when people clear from the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day or later in the afternoon, when the square is usually quieter and the light on the marble is softer. Check how the light falls on the façade when you arrive, and move a few steps if there is glare.

text.access_note: The square outside is open to walk through, but the cathedral is a working place of worship, so dress respectfully and check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements.

text.description: Nonnberg Abbey is a Benedictine convent that sits on the slope below Hohensalzburg Fortress. It was founded around 712/715 by Saint Rupert and is described as the oldest continuously existing nunnery in the German-speaking world. It is part of Salzburg's UNESCO-listed historic centre, and Maria von Trapp's story, which became The Sound of Music, began here. From the old city-wall platform on Kapuzinerberg you look across the rooftops to the abbey from a raised position, with the dome of the Kajetanerkirche at the left edge of the frame. That layering of church and convent is what makes the picture work, and it shows the abbey as part of the town rather than as a lone building. The abbey is some way off, so it will look small at the default lens (1x). Zoom in to pick it out, and keep a little rooftop and sky for context. The abbey interior is closed to visitors apart from the church and cemetery, so the views here are from outside. If you want a second angle, Nonnberggasse, at the abbey gate, looks over the Nonntal district toward the Untersberg, with the gate and walls in the foreground.
text.geographic_location: Nonnberg Abbey stands on the lower slope of the Festungsberg in Salzburg's Old Town, directly beneath Hohensalzburg Fortress and above the Nonntal district.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so walk from the Old Town towards Kapuzinerberg, the hill park on the north side of the city. From there the abbey lies about 500 m to the south. Kapuzinerberg has several paths, so follow the map to the platform itself. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the abbey closer. Use the default lens (1x) for a wider shot that includes the city rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Kapuzinerberg (platform on the old city walls near the Kapuzinerkloster). The abbey seen across the city from a raised position, with the Kajetanerkirche dome at the left edge of the frame. Near the Kapuzinerkloster. From here the abbey is to the south across the city, and the Kajetanerkirche dome sits at the left edge of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the abbey on one of the crossing points, with the Kajetanerkirche dome kept just inside the left edge. Include some rooftops in the foreground to give a sense of depth. If you want a closer, more intimate view, Nonnberggasse at the abbey gate is an alternative, with the gate and walls in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the abbey to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, or rest it on the wall, when you use the zoom.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: As a general tip, morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and clearer detail on the walls.

text.access_note: Kapuzinerberg is a public hill park; the abbey itself is closed to visitors apart from the church and cemetery, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

It works well on a phone because everything is close together, so you can get the whole scene in one frame without a long walk or complicated settings.

Start with a wide view that shows the square, the café frontage and a little of the buildings around it. Then move in for details such as the café's windows and signs. Keep a bit of the square in the frame so the picture says where it was taken. If people are in the square, a few small figures can add life and scale. Try not to point your phone straight at close-up faces, as it can feel intrusive.

Take a few steps to the side to change the angle and to keep anything from blocking the view. Check that vertical lines on the buildings look straight; gridlines help a lot here. Take a quick test shot and tap on the brightest area to stop it blowing out. Be considerate of other people and of the café's business while you take your photos.

text.description: The Mönchsberg is a long, wooded ridge that runs along the western edge of Salzburg's historic centre, and it is one of the best places to look back over the old town. It rises to 508 metres above sea level and is part of the city's UNESCO World Heritage Site. From the top you can see the old town's roofs and church towers, with mountains such as the Untersberg and the Berchtesgaden Alps in the wider panorama. That mix of rooftops, hills and distant peaks gives a phone photo plenty of depth. The plateau is a popular walking area for locals and visitors, with meadows, woods and several old fortifications that were turned into viewing points. One of them, the Humboldtterrasse, is known for its panorama toward the old town. The panorama terrace beside the modern art museum is another much-visited spot, and a lift inside the mountain has served the top since 1890. The mountain has a dramatic past too: in 1669 a rockfall onto the streets below caused great loss of life, and a mountain inspector has checked the rock face ever since. For photos, pick a clear spot along the edge, keep the skyline level using gridlines, and include a little foreground such as a wall or trees to add depth. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the view rewards both wide and close shots.
text.geographic_location: The Mönchsberg flanks the western side of Salzburg's historic centre, rising directly above the old town.
text.directions_text: Head for Salzburg's old town first, then go west up onto the Mönchsberg. A lift inside the mountain also runs to the top, so check the official site before you go. The phone icon on the map is about 770 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole view. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want a wall or trees in the foreground. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out church towers and rooftops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 770 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the rooftops or the sky matter more. Use a stone parapet or a few branches at the edge as a foreground frame. For a sweeping view, try panorama mode and pan slowly and steadily. Take a zoomed shot as well, to compress the towers and hills together.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the old town to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. Wipe the lens before shooting.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, more flattering light. In the evening, night mode can handle the lit-up old town if you brace your arms against a wall.

text.access_note: The Mönchsberg is a public recreation area, but the lift and the museum terrace may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Kapuzinerberg is the wooded hill that rises on the eastern bank of the Salzach, just north of Salzburg's historic centre. It reaches 640 metres and is part of the city's UNESCO World Heritage Site. It photographs well because it gives a calm green backdrop to the old town, and its walls, bastions and small towers give you plenty to frame. A Capuchin cloister was built on the hill between 1599 and 1605, on the site of a medieval fortress. Along the path up from Linzergasse stand 13 oratories with the Way of the Cross, built between 1736 and 1744. The fortification walls and bastions date from 1629, in the time of the Thirty Years' War. The Basteiweg runs along those walls on the southern and eastern sides of the hill, and the various views over the Altstadt are worth seeking out. The phone icon on the map is about 550 m south-west of the subject. From there the hill rises to the north-east and fills the frame with its wooded slope. If you then climb, the walls and little towers make good foreground shapes, with the town behind them. Wear shoes with a decent grip, as these are hillside paths, and give yourself time to stop and compose each shot rather than snapping on the move.
text.geographic_location: Kapuzinerberg lies on the east bank of the Salzach, to the north of Salzburg's historic city centre. One of the ways up starts from Linzergasse.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stop is listed for this spot, so start from the historic city centre of Salzburg and walk from the old town towards Linzergasse. One way up is the stone lane starting at the Franziskuspforte (Linzergasse); others start at the Imbergstiege and behind the Imberg shopping centre in Fürbergstrasse. text.description:
St Peter's Abbey is a Benedictine monastery at the foot of the Mönchsberg, founded in 696 by Saint Rupert. It is described as the oldest monastery in the German-speaking area with a continuous history since its foundation. The Romanesque church went up from about 1130 and was dedicated in 1147. Its onion-domed steeple dates from 1756, and the interior took on its Rococo look between 1760 and 1782.

For photos, the best part is the cemetery, the Petersfriedhof. Its oldest surviving graves date from 1288 and 1300, and it centres on the Late Gothic St Margaret's Chapel. Wrought-iron crosses and old gravestones sit in the foreground, the abbey church fills the middle, and Hohensalzburg Fortress rises on the cliff behind. That layered view is what makes the place work on a phone. Guides also say it is quieter than the old town streets.

Start wide, then step in. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole scene and the default lens (1x) for a calmer composition. Keep the graves low in the frame as a foreground. If you want a second angle, the small Margarethenkapelle framed by graves is worth a few frames. This is a working burial ground, so keep your distance from mourners and private graves, and take photos quietly.
text.geographic_location: St Peter's Abbey sits at the northern foot of the Mönchsberg in Salzburg. The cemetery lies at the foot of the hill below Hohensalzburg Fortress.
text.directions_text: No public-transport stop is listed for this spot. The abbey is at the northern foot of the Mönchsberg, below the fortress hill, and the cemetery lies there. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full view of graves, church and fortress together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the church tower, the fortress on the cliff, or the details of the chapel.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (inside the cemetery, looking back toward the abbey church and up toward the fortress). The abbey church and the graves in the foreground, with Hohensalzburg Fortress rising on the cliff behind. From here the graves fill the foreground, the abbey church fills the middle, and Hohensalzburg Fortress rises behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the church on one of the vertical lines. Keep the graves and crosses along the bottom edge for depth, and leave room at the top for the fortress. Crouch slightly so the foreground looks fuller. For a different view, the small Gothic Margarethenkapelle framed by graves also shows the abbey church and cathedral in the wider scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the stonework doesn't wash out. The shade under the trees and arcades can be darker than the sky, so check both before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, according to one guide, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: The cemetery is a working burial ground. Photography inside the church is restricted, and the catacombs are a separate paid visit, so check the official site before you go for access details.

Everything sits close together, so one wide frame tells the whole story.

The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) is the easiest way to fit the fountain and the cathedral into one picture. The square is open at all hours, but street performers, horse carriages and the Christmas market can crowd the fountain. Temporary stages and structures have also blocked the view at times, for example in September. In winter the fountain is sometimes boarded up, so you may not see the water at all. For the cleanest shot, go early in the morning or in the evening. As an alternative, step back into the square itself and photograph the fountain set within the open paving, with the Baroque facades and church towers framing it from the sides.

text.description:
This is a footbridge over the Salzach known for the padlocks on its railings. Its official name is Marko-Feingold-Steg, after it was renamed in 2021 from Makartsteg, and both names are used locally and on maps. Against the Old Town roofs and Hohensalzburg Fortress, the padlocks make a good foreground for a phone photo.

A recommended alternative to shooting on the bridge is the riverside quay, Elisabethkai, on the east (new town) bank next to the bridge. It is a quieter alternative that puts the bridge in a wider scene. From there the footbridge sits in the foreground, with the Old Town roofs and the fortress behind it, so you get the whole scene in one frame. The other choice is to stand on the bridge and shoot along the lock-covered railing towards the rooftops and the fortress on its cliff, with the river below.

The padlocks are removed from time to time when the railings get too heavy, so the locks you see may differ from older photos. Walk along the quay for a few minutes and try a couple of spots before you settle. Keep the bridge slightly off-centre so the fortress has room above the roofs, and watch for people walking across, who add a sense of scale.

text.description: This stop is a riverside view named Giselakai on the Salzburg map, and it works well for a relaxed phone photo. The water and the river's edge give you a simple, layered scene without any complicated setup. The phone icon on the map is about 470 m north-west of the subject. That distance helps: a gentle zoom flattens the scene and lets the near and far sides of the river stack neatly in the frame. Walk slowly along the riverside and watch how the view changes every few steps. Water gives you mirror-like reflections on calm days, and the water's edge makes a natural leading line towards the centre of the picture. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines switched on, and try one wide shot and one closer shot from the same place. Passers-by, cyclists and traffic may appear along the riverside, so wait a moment for a clear gap if you want a calm frame. Take your time, enjoy the walk, and check the light before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The spot is a riverside view named 'Giselakai' on the Salzburg map.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. Follow the riverside south-eastwards and keep the water beside you. The phone icon on the map is about 470 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole riverside scene. Switch to 2x or 3x, depending on your phone, to pull the far bank closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the water and want lots of sky and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 470 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From here the subject is far away, so use zoom rather than walking into traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the water's edge along a lower grid line so it leads the eye down the river. Keep the horizon level and leave a little space above for sky. If cyclists or cars pass through, wait for a gap or take a few shots in a row.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the scene to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo if there are ripples, boats or people moving, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people along the riverside. On grey days the water can look flat, so frame more of the surroundings.

text.access_note: This looks like an open public riverside area, but check local signs and the official site before you go.

name: Getreidegasse
label: Getreidegasse
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Museum der Moderne' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Museum der Moderne' (way/23193071): middle (60 m across).

text.description:
Getreidegasse is the old shopping street in Salzburg's Altstadt, and it is one of the city's busiest. Tall, narrow townhouses stand shoulder to shoulder, and wrought-iron guild signs hang above the shopfronts. That mix of signs, rooflines and a lane that seems to close in is why it photographs so well. The street is mentioned as far back as about 1150, when it had a different name, and it was a trading street long before it became a shopping one. Mozart was born at No. 9, and the family lived there until 1773. The building has housed a Mozart museum since 1880. Many of the houses hide passageways and courtyards, so look for gaps between the shops.

From up here you look down over the roofs onto the Getreidegasse, with the Festival Hall and the far side of the Salzach beyond. It is quieter than the street itself, and you get there by a short lift ride from the Old Town rather than a climb. Use this view for the whole-street picture. Then go down and take the close-up shots at street level, where the guild signs and Mozart's yellow facade make good details. The street is crowded from late morning, so go early if you want it clear of people.
text.geographic_location: Getreidegasse is in the Old Town (Altstadt) of Salzburg, one block back from the Salzach river.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Old Town first. The Museum der Moderne terrace is reached by a short lift ride up the Mönchsberg from the Old Town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From the terrace, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the rooftops and the line of the street. Use the default lens (1x) for the wider view with the Festival Hall and river. At street level, the ultra-wide (0.5x) suits the narrow lane and tall facades.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Museum der Moderne (viewing platform on the Mönchsberg, next to the museum). An elevated view down onto the roofs and the Getreidegasse, with the Festival Hall and the left bank of the Salzach beyond. From here you look east and down onto the roofs and the Getreidegasse, with the Festival Hall and the left bank of the Salzach beyond.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the line of the street along one of the lower grid lines, so the roofs fill the frame and the Festival Hall sits in the distance. Keep the horizon level. For an alternative, go down to the street. There you can shoot along the lane toward the western end with the guild signs on both sides, or frame Mozart's yellow birthplace as a bright accent in the middle of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the roofs to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the roofs keep their colour. At street level, hold the phone steady and take a few frames, so you have one without people walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the morning if you want the street at street level with few people, because it gets crowded from late morning through the day. The terrace is quieter, but check the lift times first.

text.access_note: Getreidegasse is an open pedestrian street, but the lift to the Museum der Moderne terrace may have its own rules or hours, so check the official site before you go.

The street is crowded from late morning through the day, so early morning is the quietest time.
Sliding the exposure down helps keep colour in the roofs when the sky is bright.
The lift to the terrace may have its own opening times or ticket rules.
